guide.title: 1 Week Beijing Itinerary
guide.description:
Travelling to Beijing as a couple, with friends, or solo? While we went during the
o ff -season, this itinerary is perfect to cover the best sightseeing spots thay
Beijing has to o ff er.

data.name: Wangfujing Street
data.description: Wangfujing Street is one of Beijing's most famous shopping streets, with a history dating back to the Ming Dynasty. It is a bustling pedestrian street that o ff ers a mix of modern shopping malls, traditional Chinese stores, and a variety of dining options. Visitors can explore a wide range of shops selling everything from international brands to local specialties. The street is also known for its vibrant night market, where visitors can sample an array of traditional Chinese snacks and street food. Wangfujing Street is not only a shopping destination but also a cultural experience, with nearby attractions such as the Wangfujing Cathedral and the Beijing Department Store. As evening approaches, go to Jingshan Park. It has a cheap admission fee and if you climb to the top, there are amazing views of Beijing and the Forbidden City at sunset.

data.name: Jingshan Park (Jingshan Gongyuan)
data.description: Jingshan Park, or Jingshan Gongyuan, is a historical park located in the heart of Beijing. Spanning over 23 hectares, it is situated just north of the Forbidden City. Originally a royal garden during the Ming and Qing dynasties, the park features a large arti fi cial hill formed from the earth excavated to create the moats surrounding the Forbidden City. Visitors can climb to the top for panoramic views of the city and the iconic Forbidden City. The park is also home to various pavilions, ancient cypress trees, and tranquil walking paths, making it a popular spot for both locals and tourists seeking peace and natural beauty in an urban setting.
data.address: 44 Jingshan W St,  � �  Xicheng District, Beijing, China, 100009

data.name: Pearl Market (Hongqiao Market)
data.description: Dongcheng, Beijing, China Tips Make sure to check out the top  fl oor where all the pearls are being sold. Right next door, you’ll spot the Temple of Heaven. There are multiple spots and religious buildings to see here, the largest and most notable being the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests. The Temple was built during the Ming Dynasty and is now an UNESCO World Heritage Site.

data.name: Temple of Heaven
data.description: To get back to the hotel, the Eastern gate has a subway station goes back to the city centre.

data.name: Beijing Ancient Observatory
data.description: The Beijing Ancient Observatory, established in 1442 during the Ming Dynasty, is one of the oldest observatories in the world. It played a crucial role in the development of Chinese astronomy and was used for celestial observations for nearly 500 years. The observatory houses a collection of ancient astronomical instruments, including armillary spheres and celestial globes, many of which were crafted by Jesuit missionaries in the 17th century. Located on a raised platform, the observatory o ff ers a glimpse into the scienti fi c advancements of ancient China and provides insight into the historical methods of astronomical study. Tips You might spot a statue of the man who made the 365 day calendar or the guy who concluded the  fi rst digits of pi! After your time with the constellations, walk down the main road to Silk Street -  a fancy shopping mall full of clothing and fabrics. Head north from here to the Temple of the Sun. The temple is actually located in a big park so you can walk around  here  for  a  bit  and  take  in  the  structures.  At  the  centre  is  the  main monument, the sacri fi ce to the sun.

data.name: Temple of the Sun
data.description: The Temple of the Sun, located in Chaoyang District, Beijing, is a historic site that dates back to the Ming Dynasty. This temple was dedicated to the worship of the sun and is part of the larger Temple of Earth complex. The site features beautifully landscaped gardens and ancient trees, providing a serene atmosphere for visitors. Architecturally, the temple showcases traditional Chinese design elements, with a striking circular structure symbolizing the heavens. It stands as a testament to China's rich cultural heritage and attracts visitors seeking both history and tranquility. Continue up the map to Dongyue temple. A note that they only take WeChat payments or cash. The shrine in the centre features the God Dongyue himself.

data.name: Beijing Dongyue Temple
data.description: Beijing Dongyue Temple is a prominent Taoist temple in Beijing, China, dedicated to the God of Mount Tai. Established during the Yuan Dynasty in 1319, it is one of the largest and oldest Taoist temples in northern China. The temple complex features over 300 rooms and halls, including the Hall of the God of Mount Tai and the Hall of the King of Hell, each adorned with intricate carvings and statues. The temple is renowned for its cultural signi fi cance and hosts the annual Dongyue Temple Fair, attracting visitors interested in traditional Chinese culture and Taoist practices. Now, if you make your way back to the city centre down the same main road, you’ll get to Dongsi Mosque, near the Dongsi subway station. U-Town shopping centre is inbetween these two locations if you need somewhere to go indoors and relax. We saw a radio-show-hosted  fl ash dance while we were in there.

data.name: Dongsi Mosque
data.description: Dongsi Mosque, situated in the Dongcheng District of Beijing, holds signi fi cant cultural and historical value for the Islamic community in China. Established in the 18th century, the mosque features traditional Chinese architectural elements combined with Islamic design, re fl ecting the unique cultural fusion. It serves as a spiritual haven for local Muslims and o ff ers insight into the religious practices and history of Islam in China. The mosque is surrounded by a peaceful courtyard, making it a serene spot for visitors seeking to explore the rich tapestry of Beijing's diverse heritage. This walking circuit can take up most of the day if you let it so once you’re done, head back to the hotel for an early night. The next few days are packed!
data.address: 13 Dongsi S St, Dongcheng, Beijing, China, 100006

data.name: Summer Palace (Yiheyuan)
data.description: The Summer Palace (Yiheyuan) is an expansive royal garden and a masterpiece of Chinese landscape design, located in Beijing's Haidian District. Covering over 700 acres, it features a stunning array of lakes, gardens, and palaces, designed primarily during the Qing Dynasty. The centerpiece is Kunming Lake, surrounded by lush greenery and well- preserved historical structures, including the Longevity Hill. Visitors can explore scenic walking paths, bridges, and pavilions, while also enjoying beautiful views of the surrounding natural landscapes. This site o ff ers a glimpse into China's imperial history and aesthetic traditions. Transport to the palace is easily achieved by subway and tram transfers, dropping you right next to the Summer Palace West Gate. From here, engage on a scenic stroll towards the North Gate. Depending on the ticket you purchase, you can stop  at  the  other  sightseeing  spots  on  the  way  like  Suzhou  Street  and  the Summer Palace Museum. You’ll have to return to the West Gate to get the tram/train back to the city but this is a great full day out. Although, look out for the crowds in peak season!

data.name: Great Wall of China
data.description: The Great Wall of China stretches over 13,000 miles and is a UNESCO World Heritage site, recognized for its immense historical signi fi cance. Constructed over several dynasties, it served as a defense barrier against invasions and as a means of border control. Visitors come to explore its breathtaking views, intricate architecture, and rich history, with various sections accessible for hiking and photography. Each portion of the wall showcases unique features, from forti fi ed towers to stunning mountain landscapes, making it one of the most remarkable feats of engineering in human history. To get to this section, meet a Mubus tour guide in advance at Subway Line 2 - Dongzhimen Station - Exit B1 for a departure at 8AM. They will take you to the Great Wall for 5 hours, where you can explore both halves of the Mutianyu section. One side is a cable car trip up and the other side features a chair-lift up and a toboggan down. The hike between tower 19 and 20 is crazy steep but trust me, you don’t want any regrets, even if you take your time and take lots of breaks. You’ll see lots of stray cats everywhere. Don’t pat them but they de fi nitely add an element of cuteness to the scenery. Doing the tour, plus both sides of the wall, we spend approximately $200AUD. Our most expensive spend on the trip but we think it was de fi nitely worth it!

data.name: Ming Tombs (Ming Shisan Ling)
data.description: The Ming Tombs, known as Ming Shisan Ling, is a historic site located in the Changping District of Beijing. This site is the fi nal resting place for 13 Ming Dynasty emperors and features a series of elaborate tombs set among beautiful landscapes. Visitors can explore the Sacred Way, lined with stone statues and sculptures, leading to the tomb complexes. The architectural grandeur and serene surroundings make it a signi fi cant cultural site, re fl ecting the rich history and traditions of imperial China. The site is part of a larger UNESCO World Heritage Site encompassing the surrounding area. Including transport, this location will take the most part of the day, especially if you choose to see the tombs further out, so spend the rest of this time wandering around the streets of Beijing and observing all the niche spots.

data.name: Forbidden City
data.description: This imperial palace is a UNESCO World Heritage site that recognises the importance of this centre of Chinese power that spans over the last  fi ve centuries. Inside, you can see the multitudes of sculptures, silks, jade, and beautiful Chinese architecture. If you have time after visiting the place, make your way to Tiananmen Square. There  is  lots  of  security  as  you  make  your  way  there.  You’ll  see  the  famed gateway to the Forbidden City here and a portrait of Chairman Mao, a Chinese communist leader and the founder of the People’s Republic of China. If you turn around, you’ll also see the Monument to the People’s Heroes that commemorates the martyrs of revolutions during the 19th & 20th centuries. Tiananmen Square (Tiananmen

data.name: Guangchang)
data.description: Tiananmen Square, located in the heart of Beijing, is one of the largest public squares in the world and a symbol of Chinese national pride. Surrounded by important buildings like the Gate of Heavenly Peace, the National Museum of China, and the Mausoleum of Mao Zedong, the square holds great cultural and historical signi fi cance. It has been the site of numerous important events and demonstrations throughout history. Visitors can see the iconic portrait of Mao Zedong as they explore the expansive area, which covers 44 hectares. The square is a focal point for both tourists and locals, making it a must-visit in Beijing.

data.name: Monument to the People's Heroes
data.description: The Monument to the People's Heroes is a ten-story obelisk located in the southern part of Tiananmen Square in Beijing, China. Erected between 1952 and 1958, it honors martyrs of revolutionary struggles from the 19th and 20th centuries. Bonus Tips While cash isn’t essential, apps like Alipay or WeChat are de fi nitely needed when paying for things in Beijing. We found that almost nowhere except the hotel took our regular Mastercard or even a travel card. Most public toilets are squat toilets and don’t have toilet paper. If that isn’t your cup of tea, you may be able to sneak into the disability/family toilet but don’t rely on this. Make use of your hotel and bring tissues with you everywhere! Most hotels have a kettle and fridge in the room, so if you’re wanting to cut costs on food, we recommend street food and convenience store items. Check if you have to book tickets in advance! Don’t get caught out, especially for things like the Forbidden City.
